set.explanation: The JVP reflects right atrial pressure. Recurrent pulmonary emboli cause pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular strain, which raises it. Dehydration lowers the JVP; aortic stenosis, an uncomplicated asthma attack and a raised left atrial pressure do not directly raise right atrial pressure (left atrial pressure does so only after long-standing pulmonary hypertension).

why: Same idea as cad-0009 (AF with a cold, pulseless leg = embolic limb ischaemia)

set.explanation: Two to five days after an (often anterior) MI, sudden haemodynamic deterioration with a new harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, radiating to the right, suggests rupture of the interventricular septum; echo shows a left-to-right shunt, and urgent surgical or device closure is needed. Papillary muscle rupture gives acute mitral regurgitation with an apical murmur radiating to the axilla (more often after inferior MI), and free-wall rupture causes tamponade without a murmur.

Troponin may be normal in the first hours of infarction, so serial measurement is needed: a rise to above the 99th centile with a dynamic change on a repeat sample (1–3 hours with high-sensitivity assays, traditionally 6 hours) supports MI. A normal ECG or a single normal troponin does not exclude MI, failure to respond to nitrates is non-specific, and T-wave inversion alone does not confirm infarction.

An ICD for primary prevention is indicated when LVEF is 35% or less at least 40 days after MI despite optimal medical therapy, in a patient with a reasonable life expectancy; the fit 80-year-old with EF 28% qualifies. VF within the first 48 hours of an acute MI and torsades caused by cocaine have reversible causes, while complete heart block and symptomatic sinus pauses need a pacemaker rather than a defibrillator.

The commonest ECG finding in pulmonary embolism is sinus tachycardia. Signs of right heart strain (S1Q3T3, right bundle branch block, right axis deviation, T-wave inversion in V1–V4) are seen mainly with large emboli and are neither sensitive nor specific. New AF can occur, but the ECG may also be completely normal.

Of the modifiable lifestyle factors, smoking has the strongest association with MI: it roughly doubles the risk, and in younger adults the relative risk is even higher, through endothelial dysfunction, thrombosis and vasospasm. Diet, obesity, inactivity and excess alcohol all contribute but less strongly, and stopping smoking halves the excess risk within a few years.

The benefit of fibrinolysis falls steeply with time: it is greatest within the first 2–3 hours, when fresh thrombus lyses easily, and small after 12 hours. Primary PCI is the better treatment and is also time-sensitive, but its benefit over fibrinolysis depends less on how quickly it is given. Aspirin, beta-blockers and heparin help, but their benefit is not strongly time-dependent in the same way.

Troponins I and T are structural components of the cardiac myofibril (the regulatory troponin complex), not enzymes. They are highly specific for myocardial injury and stay raised for 7–14 days. CK, CK-MB, AST and LDH are enzymes that leak from damaged cells and are much less cardiac-specific.

set.stem: A patient has a stent placed in his right coronary artery. On return to the ward he develops severe chest pain and becomes very unwell, and stent thrombosis is suspected. Which ECG feature would suggest that the stent has occluded?
set.explanation: Occlusion of the right coronary artery causes an inferior (II, III, aVF) STEMI, and because the RCA usually supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, it is often accompanied by bradycardia and AV block. ST elevation in I, aVL and V6 indicates a circumflex/lateral territory, V2–V5 the LAD, and AF and anterior T-wave inversion are non-specific.

Sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension after an inferior MI is typical of rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle, which has a single blood supply (from the posterior descending artery), causing acute severe mitral regurgitation. The murmur may be soft or absent because pressures equalise quickly, and echo is diagnostic. Treatment is afterload reduction, an intra-aortic balloon pump and emergency surgery.

Sudden pulseless collapse during acute ischaemia is most often due to ventricular fibrillation, which is why patients with ACS are monitored with a defibrillator available. Immediate defibrillation restores circulation in most cases. Asystole and PEA are less common primary rhythms, and free-wall rupture occurs days rather than minutes after infarction.

A capillary refill time under 2 seconds shows adequate distal perfusion and is reassuring in a claudicant. Coldness, pallor, hair loss and absent pulses indicate more advanced arterial insufficiency. Patients should also have an ankle–brachial pressure index measured (below 0.9 confirms PAD) and be given smoking cessation and statin therapy.

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) is a segmental inflammatory occlusion of small and medium arteries and veins in young heavy smokers, usually men under 40. It causes distal ischaemia, digital ulcers and superficial thrombophlebitis, and complete smoking cessation is the only treatment that halts it. Atherosclerosis is unusual at 30 without other risk factors, and Raynaud's disease causes episodic colour change without fixed ischaemia.

why: Same idea as cad-0023 (STEMI: primary PCI is the reperfusion of choice)

set.explanation: Age is the single strongest predictor of death after MI and carries the most weight in the GRACE score. Troponin concentration, heart failure, arrhythmia and cardiac arrest also matter, but a resuscitated VF arrest in the ambulance followed by prompt PCI carries a better prognosis than advanced age. Smoking is a risk factor for MI, and patients who smoke are often younger at presentation.

After a large anterior MI, transthoracic echo assesses LV systolic function (which guides ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA and ICD decisions) and detects LV apical thrombus, which requires anticoagulation. Echo also shows mechanical complications. Scar is best characterised by cardiac MRI, arrhythmias by monitoring, and left atrial thrombus by transoesophageal echo.

set.stem: A 43-year-old man with an extensive anterior myocardial infarction undergoes coronary angiography. Which angiographic features predict the greatest benefit from coronary artery bypass graft surgery?
set.explanation: The survival benefit of CABG over medical therapy is greatest in significant left main stem disease and in multivessel disease with LV systolic dysfunction; the combination of the two gives the largest absolute gain. Single-vessel or two-vessel disease with good LV function gains symptom relief rather than survival, and diffuse distal disease in diabetes is harder to graft.

set.stem: A man with an extensive anterior myocardial infarction, left main stem and triple-vessel disease is referred for coronary artery bypass surgery. The surgeon wants to know how much of the anterior wall is scar rather than viable myocardium. Which imaging modality is best?
set.explanation: Late gadolinium-enhanced cardiac MRI shows infarct scar as bright myocardium and measures its transmural extent: segments with more than 50% transmural scar are unlikely to recover after revascularisation. Echo and stress echo infer viability from wall motion and contractile reserve, CT and angiography show coronary anatomy rather than tissue, and PET or dobutamine stress echo are alternatives.

Same idea as cad-0012 (fibrinolysis has no role in NSTE-ACS)

set.explanation: Major predictors of perioperative MI are recent ACS, coronary stenting within the preceding weeks (stent thrombosis if antiplatelets are stopped), severe LV dysfunction, insulin-treated diabetes and renal impairment (the Revised Cardiac Risk Index). A peak aortic gradient of 25 mmHg indicates only mild aortic stenosis; severe AS (mean gradient over 40 mmHg) would be a major risk.

Reaching stage 3 of the Bruce protocol (about 7–9 minutes) before ischaemia appears indicates a high ischaemic threshold and a low risk of events. Poor exercise tolerance, early ST depression, poor LV function, recent-onset or post-infarct angina all indicate higher risk and favour invasive assessment.

Stopping smoking after MI reduces the risk of death and reinfarction by about a third to a half, which is larger than the benefit of any single drug. Aspirin, statins, ACE inhibitors and cardiac rehabilitation with exercise all add further benefit and should also be given.

set.stem: A 56-year-old construction worker with hypertension and a history of smoking has had 30 minutes of nausea, breathlessness and chest pressure. His initial ECG is shown. Which of the following is NOT present on this ECG?
set.explanation: The ECG shows sinus tachycardia (a P wave before every QRS) with marked ST elevation in V1–V4 and reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads: an acute anterior STEMI with inferior and posterior changes. The QRS complexes are narrow and preceded by P waves, so there is no ventricular tachycardia.

set.stem: The ECG shown is from a 56-year-old man with 30 minutes of chest pressure and breathlessness. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
set.explanation: ST elevation across the anterior chest leads (V1–V4) with reciprocal inferior ST depression indicates a proximal occlusion of the left anterior descending artery, which supplies the anterior wall and septum. RCA occlusion causes inferior ST elevation, and circumflex occlusion causes lateral or posterior changes, which are often subtle.

set.stem: A 48-year-old woman attends for a first visit. She reports 'some heart trouble' in the past and takes tablets for cholesterol and blood pressure. Her ECG is shown. Which statement about this ECG is true?
set.explanation: Pathological Q waves (wider than 40 ms or deeper than a quarter of the R wave) in contiguous leads indicate a previous transmural infarction. This ECG is not a left bundle branch block, the rhythm is not simple sinus rhythm throughout, and the T-wave changes are old changes rather than evidence of acute ischaemia. Echo can confirm a regional wall-motion abnormality.

set.stem: A 45-year-old woman who smokes, with previous breast cancer treated by mastectomy and radiotherapy, has had 6 months of breathlessness, nausea and sweating when walking up a hill. Resting ECG and examination are normal, and an exercise SPECT (technetium-99m sestamibi) perfusion scan (shown) demonstrates reversible ischaemia. Which arterial territory is most likely involved?
set.explanation: The scan shows a reversible perfusion defect (reduced uptake at stress that normalises at rest) in the apex, anterior wall and septum, which is the territory of the left anterior descending artery. Inferior defects suggest the RCA/posterior descending artery, and lateral defects the circumflex. Mediastinal radiotherapy accelerates coronary disease, particularly of the proximal LAD.

set.stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and a history of smoking had a large anterior MI 4 days ago treated with PCI to the LAD. His EF is 25%, he has had no ventricular arrhythmias, and he has bibasal crackles and a raised JVP. He takes aspirin, clopidogrel and atorvastatin. All of the following will reduce his mortality over the next 40 days EXCEPT:
set.explanation: Early after MI with LV dysfunction, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and eplerenone (EPHESUS) reduce mortality. ICD implantation in the first 40 days after MI does not reduce overall mortality (DINAMIT, IRIS), so EF should be reassessed after 40 days on optimal therapy; a wearable defibrillator can bridge high-risk patients.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: Coronary artery disease is the commonest cause of HFrEF in developed countries. About half of all heart failure is HFpEF, and 1-year mortality remains substantial (roughly 10–30%). Genetic cardiomyopathies are more common than once thought (a large share of 'idiopathic' dilated cardiomyopathy), and anaemia worsens existing heart failure but rarely causes it in a normal heart.

Angina provoked predictably by exertion and relieved by rest within minutes is stable angina. CCS class I is angina only with strenuous or prolonged exertion, class II is a slight limitation of ordinary activity (for example walking uphill or climbing stairs rapidly), class III is a marked limitation (one flight of stairs at normal pace), and class IV is angina with any activity or at rest.

A diagnostic exercise ECG needs at least 85% of the age-predicted maximum heart rate (220 − 50 = 170, so about 145 beats/min); a peak of 130 makes the test non-diagnostic. Upsloping ST depression is also less specific than horizontal or down-sloping depression of 1 mm or more. A rise in blood pressure to 155/95 mmHg during exercise is a normal response.

Recognised mechanisms of NSTE-ACS are non-occlusive thrombus on a disrupted plaque (the commonest), dynamic obstruction from spasm (Prinzmetal), progressive mechanical narrowing, inflammation, and secondary ischaemia from increased demand or reduced supply (tachycardia, anaemia, hypotension). Microvascular endothelial dysfunction causes angina with normal coronary arteries (microvascular angina), but it is not a recognised cause of NSTEMI.

set.stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and a history of smoking has had exertional chest pressure for 3 weeks, occurring with less exertion over the past week and tonight at rest, lasting about 10 minutes and radiating to the jaw. His ECG shows new T-wave inversion in I, II, aVL, V5 and V6. Which diagnosis is appropriate?
set.explanation: Crescendo angina progressing to pain at rest, with new T-wave inversion, is an NSTE-ACS. Unstable angina and NSTEMI are distinguished only by troponin: a rise means NSTEMI, normal serial values mean unstable angina. So without the troponin result the diagnosis cannot yet be finalised, although treatment (antiplatelets, anticoagulation, risk stratification) starts at once.

set.stem: A 42-year-old man with anuric diabetic end-stage renal disease missed his last dialysis and is breathless. HR 105/min, BP 185/100 mmHg, bibasal crackles and a raised JVP; the ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST deviation, and troponin I is 0.14 ng/mL (normal < 0.06). What are the most appropriate next steps?
set.explanation: A small troponin rise with volume overload, hypertension and tachycardia in an anuric dialysis patient most likely reflects myocardial injury from increased demand rather than an acute plaque event. The priority is urgent dialysis with ultrafiltration (furosemide will not work in anuria), while serial troponins and ECGs look for a rising pattern. Antiplatelets, heparin or angiography are only needed if an ACS evolves.
